items.title: Economic Order
items.hook: order the right qty, every time!
items.simple_words: EOQ is the order size at which ordering cost + carrying cost is the lowest.

definitions.meaning: Cost of placing and receiving an order: ==order processing, transport, receiving and inspection==. Falls as order size rises (fewer orders).
Cost of holding stock: ==storage, insurance, interest on capital, obsolescence==. Rises as order size rises (more average stock).

key_points: At EOQ, ==total ordering cost = total carrying cost==.
Average stock = EOQ ÷ 2 (when there is no safety stock).
Number of orders in a year = Annual demand ÷ EOQ.

formulas.name: Economic Order Quantity
formulas.legend: A = annual demand (units), O = cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year

formulas.name: Carrying cost per unit, when given as %
formulas.rhs: Purchase price per unit × Carrying cost %
formulas.legend: Always convert C to ₹ per unit per year before using it

formulas.name: Number of orders in a year
formulas.legend: Use the same annual demand A as in the EOQ formula

insight.text: Order more and carrying cost rises; order less and ordering cost rises. ==EOQ balances the two.==

memory_trick.explanation: ==2 × A × O== sits on top and ==C (Chai)== at the bottom; then take the square root of the whole thing.

steps: Convert C to ₹ per unit p.a.
items.exam_tip: If carrying cost is given as a !!% of the purchase price!!, first convert it to ₹ per unit per year.

doubt.question: Does the purchase price change EOQ?
doubt.answer: Only through C. Without a quantity discount, the purchase cost is the same at every order size, so it doesn't change EOQ.

mistakes.wrong: Taking monthly or quarterly demand as A
mistakes.right: A must be ==annual== demand: convert monthly or quarterly figures first.

mistakes.wrong: Using the carrying cost % directly as C
mistakes.right: C = purchase price per unit × carrying %, in ₹ per unit per year.
It is √(2AO ÷ C). Without the 2, the answer is EOQ ÷ √2.

items.title: Capital vs Revenue
items.hook: one wrong call changes the profit!
items.simple_words: Capital expenditure gives benefit for many years; revenue expenditure is used up within the year.

definitions.meaning: Spent to ==acquire or improve a fixed asset== or to increase earning capacity; the benefit lasts more than one year. Shown in the Balance Sheet.
Spent to ==run the business day to day== or to keep assets in working order; the benefit ends within the year. Charged to the P&L A/c.

key_points: Test: does it increase the asset's ==capacity, life or efficiency==? Yes means capital.
Repairs that only keep an asset in working order are revenue.
Freight and installation of a new machine are part of its cost: capital.

insight.text: Buying and installing it is ==capital==; servicing and repairing it later is ==revenue==.

memory_trick.explanation: Ask: =='Will this still help the business next year?'== Yes means capital; no means revenue.

items.exam_tip: Wages paid for installing a new machine are ==capital==: add them to the machine's cost, !!not to the P&L A/c!!.

doubt.question: Is every repair a revenue expense?
doubt.answer: No. Normal repairs are revenue, but a major overhaul that increases the asset's life or capacity is capital.

mistakes.wrong: Charging installation of a new machine to the P&L A/c
mistakes.right: Installation brings the asset into use: add it to the machine's cost (capital).

mistakes.wrong: Treating repairs to a newly bought used asset as revenue
mistakes.right: Repairs to make a second-hand asset fit for use are ==capital==.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking a large amount must be capital
mistakes.right: The amount doesn't decide it; the ==nature and period of benefit== do.

items.title: Offer vs
items.simple_words: An offer is ready to be accepted; an invitation only asks others to make offers.

definitions.meaning: Showing willingness to do or not to do something, to get the other person's ==assent==.
A statement that asks others to make offers, with ==no intention to be bound== on acceptance.

key_points: Quoting the lowest price is not an offer (Harvey v. Facey).
Goods displayed with price tags only ==invite offers==.
In an auction, the bidder offers; the fall of the hammer is acceptance.

insight.text: The customer makes the offer at the counter; the shopkeeper may accept or refuse it (Boots Cash Chemists).

memory_trick.explanation: ==A==uction notice, ==P==rice list or tag, ==A==dvertisement, ==C==atalogue, ==T==ender notice: each only invites offers.

items.exam_tip: In case questions, ==name the case law== and !!write a clear conclusion!!; marks are given for both.

doubt.question: Is every advertisement only an invitation?
doubt.answer: No. An advertisement promising a reward to anyone who does a set act is a ==general offer== (Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.).

mistakes.wrong: Calling a price tag on goods an offer
mistakes.right: It is an invitation to offer; the buyer makes the offer at the counter.

mistakes.wrong: Treating a tender notice as an offer
mistakes.right: The notice invites offers; each tender submitted is an offer.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the auctioneer makes the offer
mistakes.right: The bidder makes the offer; the auctioneer accepts by the fall of the hammer.
